AI is creating a global race for power. Governments are moving quickly to build generation, grids and dedicated capacity for data centres. That urgency should extend to the energy needed by schools, hospitals, farms and businesses.

On 23 September, I will join the IEEE Tech for Sustainability Summit during New York Climate Week to discuss The Role of AI in Accelerating Energy System Innovation and Transition.

The numbers show how quickly the energy landscape is changing:

Data-centre electricity consumption could almost double between 2025 and 2030, rising from around 485 TWh to 950 TWh.

More than 100 GW of new gas capacity is planned as dedicated onsite supply for data centres. Almost all of it is in the United States, with around 13 GW announced or under development elsewhere.

Middle-income countries generate around half of ChatGPT traffic, while low- and middle-income countries host only about one-quarter of global data-centre capacity.

AI is a double-edged sword for energy systems. It can improve renewable forecasting, grid management, efficiency and investment planning. It can also drive major new electricity demand, make fossil-fuel extraction cheaper and more productive, and extend dependence on existing fuels. Policies, safeguards and financing decisions will determine which effects dominate.

I look forward to discussing how countries can shape this expansion around their own development priorities: building additional clean power, strengthening grids, protecting people and ecosystems, and ensuring that the infrastructure and value created are more widely shared. #ClimateWeekNYC #ArtificialIntelligence #EnergyTransition #EnergyForDevelopment #SustainableAI

World leaders are gathering in New York at a time of profound global strain. Here is what I think the next few days should be about:

The United Nations General Assembly is one of the few places where every country, large or small, has a voice. It is where leaders come together to debate the world's biggest challenges, build coalitions and, at its best, turn diplomacy into action.

That matters especially now.

Wars are reshaping lives and economies. Climate change is accelerating. Economic uncertainty is growing. New technologies are creating extraordinary opportunities, alongside new risks.

At moments like this, the instinct can be to turn inward.
But we should do exactly the opposite.

This is a moment for cooperation over retreat.

Because the challenges crossing our borders cannot be solved by countries acting alone.

Progress does not happen by itself.
We have to choose it.
And build it. #UNGA

On Sept. 23, at #UNGA81, UNDP  will bring more than 58,000 young voices into the conversation at “Sparking the Next Generation of Energy Talent.”

Working with Goodwall , we heard directly from young people around the world on how they see their roles in the energy transition. And their engagement was encouraging:
- "Give us the skills, give us the affordable tools, and we will be powering Kenya's digital future."
- "Every hour of darkness is an hour of lost potential... In Nigeria, we have some of the most abundant sunshine on earth. We just need the will to use it."
By 2030, 1.2 billion young people are expected to enter the global workforce. Fewer than 40% are projected to have the skills needed for the green economy.

Demand for green talent is already accelerating:
☀️ Solar PV supported 7.2 million jobs globally in 2024.
💼 Workers with green skills are hired at a rate 46.6% above the workforce average.
🎓 Only 1 in 20 Gen Z workers has the green skills needed to access these opportunities.

We have listened to more than 58,000 young people about their ambitions, the opportunities they want to pursue and the barriers they face. We are bringing their voices to #UNGA81.

Creating green jobs must be matched by access to relevant skills, work experience, mentorship, networks and finance.

We need stronger links between learning and employment, skills and jobs, ideas and capital, and young talent and the industries emerging through the energy transition.
Young people are the workforce needed to deliver the transition now.

#YouthInEnergy #EnergyForDevelopment #SDG7

Why UNDP and IEEE? Why do we pursue? Why the world should care? 

As we know UNDP plays a key role providing development expertise and country-level presence driving the development agenda. This could be layered alongside IEEE’s global engineering community, technical knowledge, and standards ecosystem.

Several key opportunities we can identify here: (some personal insights here) 

We can aim to translate emerging technologies into practical solutions for energy access, climate resilience, digital inclusion, disaster preparedness, healthcare, and sustainable infrastructure.

We can ensure that technology projects respond to local development needs rather than being driven solely by technical possibilities.

We can come together and support responsible and inclusive adoption of artificial intelligence, renewable energy, smart grids, connectivity, and other digital technologies.

We can strengthen local capacity by engaging young professionals, universities, engineers, policymakers, entrepreneurs, and communities.

With the strength of IEEE in standards, we can promote standards, interoperability, cybersecurity, safety, and ethical technology deployment.

Then, we can help countries convert the Sustainable Development Goals and climate commitments into technically credible, scalable projects.

Finally, access to finance and partnerships by connecting governments and communities with technical experts, industry, academia, and international institutions.

These could be potential ways that this relationship can be utilized meaningfully for the benefit of the global community. IEEE #TSCMO UNDP Riad Meddeb Alin Iancau Julie Bernicker

The global risk landscape has changed dramatically.

Yesterday, the 2026 United Nations Global Risk Report launched at an event hosted by Ambassador Burhan Gafoor, with keynote remarks from UN Under-Secretary-General Guy Ryder and a high-level discussion moderated by Ravi Agrawal , Editor-in-Chief of Foreign Policy .

One message stands out: the world’s perception of risk is shifting and the risk landscape has gotten more complex.

In the 2024 survey, concerns centered on environmental threats, misinformation, and pandemics. Just two years later, the map has been redrawn.

🔴 Geopolitics and conflict have moved to the center of global concern.
Large-scale war is now viewed as: 
• The most interconnected global risk
• The strongest driver of other risks
• One of the most important threats facing the world today

Most strikingly, it is no longer seen as a distant possibility. It recorded the single largest jump in perceived immediacy, climbing sixteen places in expectations of how soon it could materialize.

⚡ Technology risks are rising rapidly.
Respondents expressed significantly greater concern about AI and frontier technologies, as well as the concentration of power driven by technological change. At the same time, many believe global institutions are not adequately prepared to manage these risks, particularly given growing challenges around data, information, and governance.

🌍 Environmental risks remain fundamental.
Although attention has shifted toward geopolitical threats, climate change, natural hazards, and resource shortages continue to rank among the world's most important risks. These challenges have not disappeared. They now coexist with a growing set of political and technological pressures.

🤝 The risks may be changing. The solution is not.
Perhaps the most encouraging finding is this: across regions, sectors, and perspectives, respondents consistently identify joint action as the most effective response.

In a world where risks are increasingly interconnected and increasingly imminent, cooperation is not a luxury. It is a necessity.

The 2026 Global Risk Report is a timely reminder that while our threat landscape evolves, the need for collective action remains constant.

Download the report: 👉 https://lnkd.in/gd6b29MW Many thanks to our project partner, National University of Singapore LRF Institute for the Public Understanding of Risk and Red Team members Joseph Asunka , Jakkie Cilliers , Jeanette Kwek , Trish J Lavery PhD , Clarissa Rios Rojas , Rumtin Sepasspour , Richard Smith-Bingham #GlobalRiskReport #GlobalRisks #Multilateralism #Geopolitics #ArtificialIntelligence #ClimateChange #RiskManagement #FutureOfGovernance #InternationalCooperation #UN #StrategicForesight #OurCommonFuture UN 2.0 | United Nations UN Scientific Advisory Board

Before I led UNDP's work on decarbonization and sustainable energy, I served as Senior Principal Advisor for Small Island Developing States.
 
That work taught me something: in SIDS, energy is never just infrastructure. It's sovereignty. It's fiscal space. And after a storm, it's survival.
 
On Sept. 22, I'll be joining the AEG Caribbean Energy Roundtable during Climate Week. Here's what's on my mind:
 
Over 90% of energy across SIDS is imported oil. Caribbean households pay up to 3x more for electricity than in the US.
 
In Dominica, two primary schools destroyed by Hurricane Maria were rebuilt to survive Category 5 winds, with solar microgrids that now double as hurricane shelters. In Haiti, a 120-bed hospital in Bonne Fin with no grid connection ran straight through Hurricane Matthew on solar and batteries. 
 
Decentralization isn't the second-best option for small islands. It's the resilient one.
 
The region needs roughly $1.25B a year to transition.
But actual investment has been closer to $50M.
 
The technology isn't the gap. It's capital not showing up: 
- It's aging grids that can't absorb distributed generation. 
- It's projects stalling between preparation and financing. 
- And it's fiscal space: six of the world's ten most indebted small island economies are Caribbean, while fuel imports alone consume between 7 and 12% of GDP across much of the region, and over 20% in some.

Which is why I'm looking forward to this conversation. Not another round of pledges, but a room built to move money: leaders of Caribbean heritage alongside regional public, private, and civic partners, committed to catalytic impact within 12 months.
See you there. 
 
#ClimateWeekNYC #SIDS #EnergyTransition

In 2023 it took the whole year for global battery demand to pass 1TWh. In 2026 we got there by the end of July. The latest numbers from Benchmark Mineral Intelligence show how the world delivered the same amount of storage in fewer and fewer months: 12 months in 2023, 11 in 2024, 9 in 2025 and now 7. EVs, grid storage and a long tail of smaller applications are all pulling in the same direction.
 
Stationary storage is growing particularly fast, up 28% year to date. The surprise is where that growth is coming from. Chinese demand has actually fallen by 6%, and China's share of global storage demand has dropped from 60% in 2025 to 37% so far in 2026. The rest of the world has more than made up the difference.

#AI is driving demand for digital #infrastructure at unprecedented scale.

By 2030, global data centre investment is projected to reach $7 trillion, while electricity demand is expected to grow by at least 20% each year.

But the future of data centres depends on more than technology. Their long-term viability also relies on the energy, water and infrastructure systems around them, and the confidence of the communities that host them.

A new World Economic Forum paper, Data Centre Sustainability and Resilience: A Decision Playbook for AI Infrastructure, produced in collaboration with Oliver Wyman, provides a practical framework for making more sustainable and resilient decisions across the data centre lifecycle.

Built around four practical questions, it offers tools and metrics that can help stakeholders make informed capital decisions, reduce the risk of costly redesign and adapt as technologies and operating environments evolve.

With the start of UNGA, electrification is moving to the centre of the development agenda. 

Are we able to move from ambition to implementation?


“35 by 35” captures the scale of the challenge: increasing electricity’s share of global final energy consumption from just over 20% today to 35% by 2035.

Tomorrow, at #UNGA81, on September 22, the COP31 Presidency, the International Energy Agency (IEA)  and the United Nations will convene the third High-Level Energy Transitions Solutions Dialogue during UNGA High-Level Week.

The discussion will focus on the systems needed to support electrification across transport, buildings and industry, including stronger grids, storage and flexibility:

* Global grid investment is expected to reach around US$550 billion in 2026, up 17% in one year, although higher equipment costs account for part of this growth.
* Battery storage investment is expected to exceed US$100 billion.
* More than 2,500 GW of renewable generation, storage and large-load projects are waiting in grid connection queues worldwide.

The dialogue will also address energy efficiency, clean cooking and energy security, with a focus on moving these priorities into national plans, investment pipelines and implementation.

UNDP  is supporting countries to translate global energy ambitions into country-level delivery and impact at scale.

I look forward to the discussion around advancing the systems, financing and partnerships required to deliver 35 by 35.

#UNGA81 #COP31 #EnergyTransition #Electrification #EnergySecurity

HOT OFF THE PRESS: For the first time ever, the IEA has published a dedicated Electrification Report. It is an absolute treasure trove of data. Here are some of the key takeaways that stood out to me when I peer-reviewed it.

1) Electrofficiency: The headline electrification rate undersells electricity's real role. Electricity is 23% of final energy, but it delivers almost 40% of useful energy - the heat, mobility, cooling and light people actually need. That is because electric technologies waste far less than fossil fuels. In the High Electrification Scenario, electricity reaches 35% of final energy by 2035 but supplies over half of all useful energy.

2) Transport has large potential. Battery prices have fallen 90% since 2010. Around half of oil-based road transport could be electrified competitively today. If battery costs keep falling, that rises to over four-fifths.

3) Heat pumps can compete in most places that need heat. They are competitive in around 75% of heating markets across advanced economies and China. Half of global space heating demand could be electrified cost-effectively.

4) Industry is the sleeping giant. Around 40% of energy used for low- and medium-temperature industrial heat can be electrified cost-effectively right now. More in the future.

5) Electrification is an energy security strategy. EVs already avoid 2.3 million barrels of oil a day. That is more than the volume that bypassed the Strait of Hormuz via the Habshan-Fujairah pipeline this summer. In the High Electrification Scenario, importers cut their fuel bills by USD 400 billion a year by 2035.

The gap is policy. Under current settings, electrification only reaches around 30% by 2035. Very few countries have a comprehensive, cross-sectoral electrification strategy. Grids need to expand 40% faster than over the past decade.

Full report here: https://lnkd.in/eiZby9TS

Yesterday, at the International Renewable Energy Agency (IRENA) we published the third edition of the Tracking report on the UAE Consensus goals, and I've been going back through it.

The headline is good news, with a record of 693 GW of renewable capacity added in 2025, and the gap to tripling by 2030 narrowed to about 0.6 TW.

The part I keep coming back to is further in, and is bringing some hope to all of us working on accelerating a renewables-powered energy transition: 
- Factories can now make more than twice as many solar modules as the world is buying.
- Most new renewable capacity is cheaper than the cheapest fossil alternative. 

The technology is there, and it's cheap.

And yet, of those 693 GW, Africa added 11.3. Central and West Africa together added 0.4, while G20 countries account for around 91% of the investment.

So in a lot of these markets the problem isn't the price of panels. It's the price of money. 

The report is direct about it: country, currency and regulatory risk keep capital away, and what helps is guarantees, de-risking, concessional finance and buyers for the power that a lender can trust.

For those of you on the financing side: in your experience, what moves things more in these markets: is it a cheaper capital, or a more reliable buyer for the power?

Source: IRENA (2026), Delivering on the UAE Consensus

What is the development return on a clean cookstove?

Yesterday, UNDP  joined the first High-Level Event on Clean Cooking at the UN General Assembly, convened by Kenya and Norway with support from the International Energy Agency (IEA).

Africa is expanding clean cooking access faster than ever. In 2024, progress was three times faster than in 2010. Yet population growth meant that, by year’s end, 14 million more people were relying on wood and charcoal.

Polluting cooking costs the world more than US$2.4 trillion each year. Universal access would require around US$8 billion annually through 2030.
We are paying trillions to avoid investing billions.

Clean cooking requires more than distributing stoves. It needs fuels, finance, infrastructure, local businesses and services that households can depend on every day.

More than 120 clean cooking policies have been introduced across Africa over the past two years. Through Mission 300, its partnership with UNCDF and a portfolio reaching more than 2.5 million people, UNDP is helping turn that momentum into functioning markets and investable programmes.

The return is cleaner air, time returned to women and girls, stronger local businesses and more resilient economies.

The return is measured in lives saved, hours reclaimed by women and girls, businesses built and forests protected. At US$8 billion a year, the question is why we continue to pay US$2.4 trillion instead.

#CleanCooking #EnergyAccess #SustainableDevelopment #GenderEquality #Mission300

74% of participants wanted to explore clean energy careers. 56% asked how to start.

These are findings from UNDP and Goodwall’s conversations with more than 58,000 young people across over 180 countries. One participant described people travelling long distances just to charge their devices. With 655 million people still without electricity, that journey says a great deal about who can access the digital economy.

Today, we brought public and private sector partners together to discuss how to close the skills gap and bring clean energy jobs to places that need them most.

Renewable energy already employs 16.6 million people, but more than 85% of those jobs are concentrated in five countries and regions. The talent is far more widely distributed.

Young people proposed businesses ranging from solar-powered kitchens to sustainable energy consultancies. They also asked for practical ways to learn the skills those ideas require. UNDP’s upcoming Sustainable Energy Academy will offer more than 40 hours of modules spanning energy finance and governance, access and efficiency, data and technology, and the climate-energy nexus.

As a young man from the Philippines told us: “Invest not only in clean energy technologies, but also in the young people who build them. Because when we power communities with clean energy, we don't just light homes, we ignite opportunities.”

Every year of delay leaves communities without reliable power and holds back the people ready to build a cleaner energy future.

Tomorrow, UNDP  and Goodwall  will release "Powering the Future," our full report on the careers young people want to pursue, the businesses they want to build, and what they need to get started.

#CleanEnergyJobs #YouthEmployment #EnergyAccess #JustEnergyTransition #SDG7

The world is planning for a surge in electricity demand. 

How can this be turned into an opportunity for energy security and socio-economic resilience?

Yesterday, UNDP  joined the COP31 Türkiye –IEA–UN High-Level Energy Transition Solutions Dialogue at UN Headquarters. The IEA also released new analysis prepared for the COP31 discussions.

Its findings point to the scale of the opportunity. Electricity could cost-effectively meet 33% of global final energy use by 2035, up from 23% today, putting the proposed 35% goal within reach. In a faster electrification scenario, fuel-importing countries could cut their energy import bills by more than US$400 billion by 2035—reducing exposure to volatile fossil-fuel markets and strengthening energy security.

Accelerating electrification can create a broader development dividend. Investment in renewable energy, grids, storage and clean technologies can support green jobs, build domestic value chains and drive green industrialization, to power that businesses and communities need to grow.

But realizing this opportunity will require investment in generation and grids, while addressing the upfront costs that can prevent households and businesses from benefiting. Around 1.18 billion people still experience energy poverty, while Africa receives only 2% of global clean energy investment.

UNDP is supporting this effort alongside around 30 UN entities, with the aim of helping at least 100 countries build the policies and project pipelines needed to put finance to work.

The opportunity is not simply to electrify more of the global economy, but to use electrification to build more secure, resilient and inclusive economies. By 2035, can we ensure that growing electricity demand translates into new industries and green jobs, while also delivering reliable and affordable energy to hospitals, businesses and households?

Read the International Energy Agency (IEA)  analysis here: https://lnkd.in/geS9jit6

#UNGA #COP31 #EnergyTransition #SDG7

Everyone is asking who will win the AI race. During yesterday’s IEEE Tech for Sustainability Summit in New York, I posed a different question: what does winning actually mean?

For me, the answer starts with energy.

AI could help unlock up to 175 GW of capacity from existing transmission lines. Across the Global South, companies are already using it for grid optimisation, smart metering, forecasting and industrial efficiency.

But the same technology can push in the opposite direction. AI is also making oil and gas exploration faster and cheaper, with recent modelling suggesting the resulting emissions could be 3.3 to 13.3 times larger than estimated 2025 data-centre emissions.

So the question is not whether AI is efficient. It is what AI is making more efficient.

This matters when 91% of new utility-scale renewable projects are already cheaper than the cheapest new fossil alternative. In Pakistan, low-cost solar imports helped avoid more than $12 billion in fuel imports. In Chile, financing for the 151 MW Calama wind farm was linked to emissions avoided through early coal retirement.

AI will add another major source of electricity demand. Whether that extends the age of energy addition or accelerates the transition will depend on choices around grids, finance, standards and public policy.

And who captures the value?

Middle-income countries generate more than 40% of ChatGPT traffic, yet middle- and low-income countries host only around 27% of shared data-centre facilities.

A sustainable AI framework must therefore ask what AI enables across the economy, where infrastructure is built, who owns the capabilities, and what countries gain in return.

Human intelligence created this wave. The task now is to decide where we direct it.

We explore these questions further in UNDP’s The Energy Sprint of the AI Race: A Green Window of Opportunity for Developing Countries?
https://lnkd.in/gUFFVVgS

#EnergyforDevelopment #NewYorkClimateWeek

export-urn-li-share-7509308070745804800.caption:
Which country, after Norway, had the highest share of electric cars in new car sales last year? Nepal, at 68%.

I opened with that question at today’s SDG7 Action Forum in New York. We often describe SDG7 through its gaps: 655 million people without electricity and two billion without clean cooking. But that account misses how quickly energy markets are changing.

Solar’s share of global electricity has risen from 1% to around 9% in a decade. Developing and emerging economies will account for 85% of electricity demand growth through 2035. Three priorities follow:

Build the systems around the power. Africa is heading for around 17 GW of new solar this year. Grids and storage must keep pace. In Mauritius, UNDP  has supported smart-grid technology and 18 MW of battery storage.

Lower financing costs. The same solar project can face two to three times the cost of capital in many emerging economies. A one percentage point reduction could save US$150 billion a year.

Keep more value locally. Electricity should power farms, businesses, and industry. Yet of 16.6 million renewable energy jobs worldwide, only 344,000 are in Africa.

By 2030, how much of the transition’s value will stay in the countries producing its power?

#SDG7 #EnergyforDevelopment #UNGA81

🏝️ One of Sicily's main cities just did something no municipality has done before.
 
🤝 Agrigento has signed on to become the first local administration in the world to join the 100x100 Campaign, applying the same island-led approach that's driving renewable transitions from Curaçao to Tonga, to a mainland Italian town.
 
⚡ The city faces real pressure: recurring power outages, wildfires straining the grid, energy prices above the EU average, all set against the backdrop of the Valley of the Temples.
 
🎯 Rather than wait, Agrigento is taking the lead, committing to 100% renewable energy by 2045 or sooner, guided by Greening the Islands Foundation and Blue Planet Alliance through a comprehensive roadmap covering technology, policy and finance, and its hands-on implementation on the ground, setting an example for Sicily and for towns across Italy and beyond.
 
🌍 This is what bottom up climate governance looks like: local communities, who understand their own vulnerabilities best, driving the solutions.
 
✍️ The MoU was signed in New York during Climate Week, making Agrigento the first municipality to join as a case study of a local community taking the lead on its own energy transition towards 100% RES, an approach welcomed by International Renewable Energy Agency (IRENA), UNDP, Global Solar Council (GSC) and Global Renewables Alliance (GRA).
 
🔗 Full press release, link in comments.

A.C.C.T© Forum: Advancing Africa’s Clean Cooking Transition Through Solutions, Finance & Collaboration

The African Clean Cooking Transition Forum (ACCT©) brought together policymakers, government leaders, development partners, energy experts, innovators and civil society leaders to address one of Africa’s most pressing energy-access challenges: accelerating the transition to clean cooking.

The forum opened with remarks from Mr. Louis Cheick SISSOKO, Presiding Officer of the African Union ECOSOCC), followed by reflections from the Forum Chair, H.E Ambassador Prof. Olufolake Abdulrazaq, and Co-Chair, H.E. Ms. Macenje Mazoka .

A central panel discussion, “Solutions and Financing for Clean Cooking in Africa,” examined the role of innovation, investment, financing mechanisms and practical delivery models in expanding access to clean cooking. 

The discussion was moderated by Joy Osomiamhe-O, Executive Director of G-SEL Network and Convener of the ACCT© Forum.

The programme also featured a keynote address by Mr. Riad Meddeb of UNDP, alongside ministerial and goodwill remarks from government leaders across Nigeria, Mozambique and Tanzania.

A key highlight was the presentation of the Lagos State Clean Cooking Pilot by Mrs. Titilayo Oshodi MCIPM, FISMN, demonstrating how subnational action and innovative approaches can contribute to the wider clean cooking transition.

The forum concluded with a signing ceremony and commitments toward continued collaboration, followed by closing remarks and next steps from the Convener.

The ACCT© Forum reinforced an important message: the transition to clean cooking requires more than commitments—it requires finance, innovation, policy, partnerships and solutions that can reach the households and communities that need them.

G-SEL Network remains committed to convening the conversations and partnerships needed to turn these commitments into meaningful impact.

CONVEY . INNOVATE . IMPACT

#ACCT© #CleanCooking #EnergyAccess #WomenInEnergy #EnergyTransition #SustainableEnergy #ClimateAction #GSELNetwork #Africa
